proof.text: Use matrices as finite families of entries, as in [def-weil-matrix], with $(UV)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^r U_{ik}V_{kj}$ and identity entries $\delta_{ij}$. Let $q:R\to R/I$ send an element to its additive coset. Every coset has a representative, so choose representatives for the finitely many entries of $\overline B^{-1}$ to obtain $C$; when $r=0$ there are no choices. For the rest of the proof let $C$ be any such lift. The quotient operations are $q(x+y)=q(x)+q(y)$ and $q(xy)=q(x)q(y)$. Applying these entrywise to the finite product sums gives $\overline{BC}=\overline B\,\overline C=1$ and $\overline{CB}=\overline C\,\overline B=1$. Thus $N_{ij}=(BC-1)_{ij}$ and $P_{ij}=(CB-1)_{ij}$ have zero coset, which means precisely that they belong to $I$.

proof.text: Every summand $N_{ik}N_{kj}$ and $P_{ik}P_{kj}$ is zero by the hypothesis on pairs of elements of $I$. Hence, entrywise, $(N^2)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^r N_{ik}N_{kj}=0$ and $(P^2)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^r P_{ik}P_{kj}=0$, so $N^2=P^2=0$. The matrix identities used below are the ring identities: distributivity follows by distributing each finite sum, and associativity follows from $\sum_{k,l}(U_{ik}V_{kl})W_{lj}=\sum_{k,l}U_{ik}(V_{kl}W_{lj})$ and reordering finite sums in the additive abelian group of $R$. Identity multiplication follows by summing $\delta_{ij}$. None of these calculations changes the order of scalar factors.

proof.text: Since $BC=1+N$, associativity and distributivity give $$B\bigl(C(1-N)\bigr)=(BC)(1-N)=(1+N)(1-N)=1-N+N-N^2=1.$$ Similarly, $CB=1+P$ gives $$\bigl((1-P)C\bigr)B=(1-P)(CB)=(1-P)(1+P)=1+P-P-P^2=1.$$ Thus the proposed matrices are respectively a right and a left inverse of $B$.

source.place: Proposition 6.8.4(1), p.59, proof (1) left to the reader; explicit elementary square-zero matrix calculation supplied here

proof.text: Their equality follows by expanding the correction terms, without any commutativity assumption: $$C(1-N)=C-C(BC-1)=C-(CBC-C),$$ $$ (1-P)C=C-(CB-1)C=C-(CBC-C).$$ Their common value therefore satisfies both inverse identities from step 3 and is a two-sided inverse of $B$. For $r=0$, matrices have no entries, the unique matrix is both $0$ and $1$, and all the entrywise equalities and displayed identities remain valid.

title: square zero matrix lift
statement:
Let $R$ be a unital ring and $I$ a two-sided ideal (an additive subgroup stable under left and right multiplication by arbitrary elements of $R$) such that $xy=0$ for all $x,y\in I$. Write $R/I$ for its quotient ring of additive cosets. Let $r\geq0$ be finite and $B\in M_r(R)$ a square matrix [def-weil-matrix]. If its entrywise reduction $\overline B\in M_r(R/I)$ has a two-sided inverse, then $B$ has a two-sided inverse. More precisely, for any matrix $C\in M_r(R)$ lifting $\overline B^{-1}$ entrywise, set $N=BC-1$ and $P=CB-1$. Then
$$B\bigl(C(1-N)\bigr)=1,\qquad\bigl((1-P)C\bigr)B=1,\qquad C(1-N)=(1-P)C.$$
Thus the displayed common matrix is an inverse of $B$.
